record.original_question: What is the maximum integer N for which there exists a packing array PA(N,14,9), meaning an N x 14 array with entries from {0,1,...,8} such that every 2-column subarray contains each ordered pair of symbols at most once?

evidence.quote: A "Packing Array" PA(N,k,v) is an N x k array (N rows and k columns), with each entry from the v-set {0,1,...v-1}, so that every N x 2 subarray contains every ordered pair of symbols at most once. Given (N,k,v), we want to construct PA(N,k,v).
The upper bound is N <= 21 [Colbourn and Dinitz, 2006], so it is an open question whether N = 21 is possible.
It succeeds in constructing a Packing Array with N = 21 for k = 14 v = 9, fully resolving this open question.

artifact.self_contained_problem: A packing array PA(N, k, v) is an N × k array with entries from the alphabet {0, 1, …, v−1} such that, for every choice of two distinct columns i and j, every ordered pair (a, b) ∈ {0, …, v−1}² appears in at most one row of the resulting N × 2 subarray (i.e., there is at most one row r with the entry in column i equal to a and the entry in column j equal to b). Determine the maximum integer N for which a packing array PA(N, 14, 9) exists.
artifact.status_search_result: Standard upper bounds in the combinatorial design literature give N ≤ 21 for PA(N,14,9). A recent construction reportedly achieves N = 21, matching the upper bound and thus determining the maximum to be 21. General web search confirmed the definition and existence of upper-bound tables but did not surface independent verification beyond the construction announcement.

status_evidence.title: Packing Arrays
status_evidence.snippet: Direct and recursive constructions and upper bounds for packing arrays PA(N,k,v) are developed, with tables of best known bounds.
status_evidence.claim: Standard reference establishing the framework giving the upper bound N ≤ 21 for PA(N,14,9).
